warmup.q: A payment and its refunds obey one rule: the refunds never add up to more than the payment. Where can one write check that rule and apply a refund, with no transaction around it?
options: Only in a relational database, inside a transaction
In a MongoDB document that embeds the refunds, or in a PostgreSQL row whose jsonb column holds them: one guarded update of one record
Only in MongoDB, because PostgreSQL can't change part of a JSON value
Nowhere: a rule over several refunds always needs a multi-record transaction
warmup.why: Both stores make a write to one record atomic. Put the refunds inside the record and the rule is about one record, so a single update can check it in its filter and apply the change in the same step. PostgreSQL changes part of a jsonb value with jsonb_set. Keep refunds in their own rows or documents and the rule spans records, and then it does need a transaction.

sections.h: A document holds one payment and everything read with it
sections.html:
Lesson 5's rows each hold flat columns. The document model goes one step further: one record is a whole tree, so everything a screen shows can live in one place. In Oracle, a payment with two refunds is three rows in two tables, and the payment screen joins them. MongoDB stores a document instead: one JSON-like tree with nested objects and arrays. On disk and on the wire it's BSON, binary JSON, which adds the types JSON lacks: 32- and 64-bit integers, Decimal128, a date (UTC milliseconds), ObjectId and binary data. Every document has an _id, its primary key, unique in its collection, and a document can be at most 16 MB.

Build the payment one version at a time. Version 1 copies the tables: a payments collection and a refunds collection, each refund holding its payment's id. The screen now makes two reads. Worse, the rule "refunds never add up to more than the payment" spans two documents, so checking and writing it safely needs a multi-document transaction (the Transactions track's lesson on transactions in NoSQL).

Version 2 puts the refunds inside the payment, in an array, next to a running total, refundedMinor. One read returns everything the screen shows. And a write to one document is atomic in MongoDB: a single updateOne can check the rule and change the document, and no other write can slip in between. The refund in the Try-it is one update whose filter says "only if refundedMinor plus this refund is at most amountMinor", and whose update pushes the refund and adds to the total. Two refunds that race for the last 1,000 can't both win, because the second one's filter no longer matches. That's lesson 2's rule at work: embed what's read and changed together and stays bounded (a payment has a handful of refunds at most), reference what grows without limit.

Types matter more than they look. mongosh stores a small whole number as a 32-bit int, and a Kotlin Long sent through the Java driver becomes a 64-bit long. An amount that arrives as the string "42.50" from an old import job is stored as a string, and every sum then skips it.

That's where "NoSQL means no schema" goes wrong. A collection has no fixed columns, but you can attach a validator, a $jsonSchema that every write must pass, or MongoDB rejects it with error 121, "Document failed validation", and says which rule failed. The default level, strict, checks every insert and update, but not the documents already there. MongoDB 9.0 added a stricter level, constraint: to switch it on, MongoDB scans the whole collection and refuses if any document breaks the rules, and from then on it guarantees that every document passes. MongoDB 9.0 also checks every incoming BSON document by default, so a malformed one is refused at the door. The Try-it trips over the old string.

In MongoDB the document is the unit of everything: a write is atomic for one document, an index entry points at one document, a pipeline passes documents from stage to stage, and a replica set copies document changes in the order one primary applied them. The sections below take them in turn, with a stop in PostgreSQL before the last one.

ONE update: MongoDB checks the filter and applies it to one document atomically const refund = (id, amount) => db.payments.updateOne( { _id: "pay-81002", status: "SETTLED", $expr: { $lte: [{ $add: ["$refundedMinor", amount] }, "$amountMinor"] } }, { $push: { refunds: { refundId: id, amountMinor: amount, at: new Date() } }, $inc: { refundedMinor: amount } }) refund("ref-1", 6000).modifiedCount least 1, one of three statuses, a real date const rule = { $jsonSchema: { bsonType: "object", required: ["accountId", "merchantId", "status", "amountMinor", "createdAt"], properties: { status: { enum: sections.h: An index is a sorted list of keys that point at documents
sections.html:
Lesson 2 built the index for AP3, { merchantId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 }, and its cost() helper boiled explain() down to four numbers. Each number comes from one part of the plan, and reading plans is a daily skill.

An index is a sorted list of keys, each pointing at one document's record. IXSCAN walks a range of that list, and keysExamined counts the keys it touched. FETCH loads the document behind each key, and docsExamined counts those. COLLSCAN reads every document in the collection. SORT sorts in memory, because the order the query wants isn't an index order. A healthy query has keys examined, documents examined and documents returned close together, as lesson 2's 5, 5 and 5. When thousands of keys or documents are read to return five, the index doesn't match the query.

A query can skip the documents altogether. If it asks only for fields the index holds, and leaves out _id, MongoDB answers from the index alone. That's a covered query: the plan says PROJECTION_COVERED and docsExamined is 0. A screen that lists only times and amounts can be served that way.

Arrays get one index entry per element. An index on refunds.refundId is a multikey index: a payment with three refunds has three entries, each pointing at the same payment. "Which payment owns refund ref-1?" becomes a one-key lookup. Every write pays for every entry, so a payment with 20 refunds updates 20 entries in that index.

AP4, the idempotency key, needs a unique index, and it hides a trap. A document without the field is indexed as if the field were null, and a unique index allows only one null, so on a collection where most payments have no key the index can't even be built. Make it partial, indexing only documents where the field is a string, and a second use of the key fails with error E11000, "duplicate key".

Each index is another sorted list that every insert and update must maintain. Lesson 2's rule holds here too: add one for an access pattern you've written down, and check with explain() that the query uses it.

steps: In the same mongosh session (cost() from lesson 2's seed is still defined), run the block below one statement at a time.

sections.h: The aggregation pipeline passes documents from stage to stage
sections.html:
Finance wants M-0042's day: how many payments per status, the total amount, the largest one. In SQL that's a GROUP BY. MongoDB's answer is the aggregation pipeline: an array of stages, where each stage takes documents in and passes documents on, in order.

The stages map onto SQL closely enough to translate by hand. $match is WHERE. $group is GROUP BY, with accumulators such as $sum, $avg and $max for the aggregates; its _id is the grouping key. $sort is ORDER BY, $project is the select list, and $limit is FETCH FIRST. $unwind turns one document with an array into one document per element, which is how you'd total refunds across payments. $lookup is a left outer join to another collection.

Order matters, because each stage only sees what the previous one passed on. Put $match first and the query planner can use an index for it, so only the matching documents enter the pipeline. The Try-it's plan shows it: GROUP > FETCH > IXSCAN, 202 keys and 200 documents for M-0042's 200 payments. The AP3 index serves the match on merchantId, then has to skip over the status field it doesn't care about, which costs the two extra keys. In MongoDB 9.0 the newer execution engine runs the $group inside that same plan.

$group and $sort are blocking: they have to see every input document before they can emit anything, so they hold state in memory. Each stage may use 100 MB before it must spill to disk, and MongoDB 9.0 adds a limit for a whole operation: 1 GB or 20% of the server's memory, whichever is bigger. A report over a year of payments should $match the smallest slice it can, as early as it can.

Take a position on $lookup. It's fine for a report that runs now and then. If a hot path joins on every read, the document has the wrong shape: embed the data, or copy the few fields the read needs, the way lesson 2 copied a summary of recent payments into the account.

[s.stage, ...chain(s.inputStage)] : [] ({ plan: chain(c.queryPlanner.winningPlan.queryPlan).join(" > "), keysExamined: c.executionStats.totalKeysExamined, docsExamined: c.executionStats.totalDocsExamined })

sections.h: The same document in PostgreSQL: a jsonb column
sections.html:
You've now seen a document's write, its indexes and its pipeline. The SQL track's lesson on JSONB kept the risk engine's output in a jsonb column. That's the document model inside a relational database, and putting it next to MongoDB shows what the model buys and what the product adds.

Store the payment as one row of payment_doc(id text PRIMARY KEY, doc jsonb NOT NULL), refunds inside doc. The refund is still one statement on one record:

UPDATE payment_doc
   SET doc = jsonb_set(
               jsonb_set(doc, '{refundedMinor}', to_jsonb((doc->>'refundedMinor')::bigint + 6000)),
               '{refunds}', doc->'refunds' || '{"refundId": "ref-1", "amountMinor": 6000}')
 WHERE id = 'pay-81002'
   AND doc->>'status' = 'SETTLED'
   AND (doc->>'refundedMinor')::bigint + 6000 <= (doc->>'amountMinor')::bigint;

One UPDATE is atomic for its row. When two refunds race, the second waits for the first's row lock, then PostgreSQL checks its WHERE again against the new version of the row, so two refunds of the last 6,000 can't both pass. That's the same guarantee as MongoDB's guarded updateOne.

Validation maps too. A CHECK constraint is schema-on-write for the parts of the document you name: CHECK (jsonb_typeof(doc->'amountMinor') = 'number'). ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT scans the table and refuses if any row breaks the rule, which is what MongoDB 9.0's constraint level does. Add NOT VALID and it checks only new writes, like strict, until VALIDATE CONSTRAINT checks the old rows later.

The differences are in what surrounds the document. PostgreSQL has real joins, a cost-based optimizer and transactions over any rows, so the document can sit next to the ledger and the merchant table. Its GIN index answers containment (@>) on any key, but not ranges or order, so the fields you sort by usually stay in ordinary columns next to doc. MongoDB indexes paths inside the document in sorted order, caps a document at 16 MB, and shards a collection over many machines on its own, which one PostgreSQL primary doesn't. Both rewrite the whole stored document when you change one field, so both want small documents.

Take a position. If the documents live beside relational data, a jsonb column in the database you already run is usually the better choice. Choose MongoDB when the documents are the system: the main records, read and written whole, at a size or write rate that will need sharding.

sections.h: A replica set: one primary orders the writes, and a majority decides what survives
sections.html:
A single mongod runs on one machine, and when that machine dies, payments stop. So production MongoDB is a replica set: normally three members holding copies. One member, the primary, takes every write, applies it and records it in its oplog, a capped collection (local.oplog.rs) of changes in the order the primary applied them. The secondaries pull the oplog and replay it. This is leader-based replication: one copy decides the order and the others follow it. Cassandra in lesson 5 does the opposite, with every replica taking writes and timestamps deciding.

If the secondaries hear nothing from the primary for electionTimeoutMillis, 10 seconds by default, one of them calls an election and needs a majority of votes, 2 of 3. Two sides of a network cut can't both hold a majority, so there's never a second primary taking writes for long.

When may the client hear "OK"? That's the write concern. w: 1 acknowledges once the primary has the write; w: "majority", the default since MongoDB 5.0, waits until a majority of members have it. The difference shows in a failover, and the stepper walks through it. A member votes only for a candidate whose oplog is at least as recent as its own, so a write a majority holds survives. A write only the old primary had is rolled back when that member rejoins and saved to files under <dbpath>/rollback/, and the client that got its OK is never told. Leave payments at w: "majority" and treat a wtimeout error as "unknown", not "failed".

The Replication track builds leader-based replication from scratch in its first lesson, and the Partitioning track's lesson on running MongoDB covers setting up a replica set, sharding and the balancer.

try.title: Lose an acknowledged write in a failover
steps: Make sure env/mongo.yml is down. From the labs folder, start a three-member replica set (about 30 seconds, about 1.5 GB of Docker memory). env/mongo-rs.yml starts the members, initiates rs0 from mongo1's healthcheck and reports healthy once mongo1 is primary.
Run the commands below in order. Step 2 has to run within about 10 seconds of the disconnect, before mongo1 notices it's alone. Predict which of the four payments are left at the end.
The last command stops the set and deletes its data.

code.title: from the labs folder
code.html: docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml up -d --wait # 1. a payment that every member gets: w:"majority" docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh sfz --quiet --eval 'db.payments.insertOne({_id: "pay-81701", amountMinor: 18000}, {writeConcern: {w: "majority"}})' # 2. cut mongo1 off, then at once write to it: one w:1 write, one w:"majority" write docker network disconnect sfz-mongo-rs_default sfz-mongo-rs-mongo1-1 docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh sfz --quiet --eval 'db.payments.insertOne({_id: "pay-81723", amountMinor: 2500}, {writeConcern: {w: 1}})' docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh sfz --quiet --eval 'db.payments.insertOne({_id: "pay-81724", amountMinor: 1200}, {writeConcern: {w: "majority", wtimeout: 5000}})' # 3. wait for the election, look from both sides, write to the new primary sleep 15 docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo2 mongosh --quiet --eval 'rs.status().members.map(m => m.name + " " + m.stateStr).join("\n")' docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh --quiet --eval 'const h = db.hello(); ({isWritablePrimary: h.isWritablePrimary, primary: h.primary})' docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo2 mongosh "mongodb://mongo2:27017,mongo3:27017/sfz?replicaSet=rs0" --quiet --eval 'db.payments.insertOne({_id: "pay-81730", amountMinor: 4250}, {writeConcern: {w: "majority"}})' # 4. heal the cut, give mongo1 time to rejoin, then see what is left docker network connect --alias mongo1 sfz-mongo-rs_default sfz-mongo-rs-mongo1-1 sleep 25 docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh --quiet --eval 'rs.status().members.map(m => m.name + " " + m.stateStr).join("\n")' docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh "mongodb://mongo1:27017,mongo2:27017,mongo3:27017/sfz?replicaSet=rs0" --quiet --eval 'db.payments.find().toArray()' docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 bash -c 'ls -R /data/db/rollback; bsondump --quiet /data/db/rollback/*-*/removed.*.bson' docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml down -v

mongo1 acknowledged pay-81723 at once, though it was already cut off. The majority write waited 5 seconds and failed. Within about 15 seconds mongo2 was primary and mongo1 had stepped down: isWritablePrimary: false. After the cut healed, pay-81723, which a client was told was written, is gone from the collection; it survives only in mongo1's rollback file, together with the "failed" pay-81724. The directory name is the collection's UUID and will differ on your machine; the local.oplog.rs folder holds the undone oplog entries. mongo1 is primary again at the end because env/mongo-rs.yml gives it priority 2: once it had caught up, it called an election and took the role back. The two majority writes survived everything.

refs.title: MongoDB: rollbacks during replica set failover
MongoDB: write concern (w, wtimeout, the majority default)

analogy: Think of a bank branch with one head teller and two assistants. Every transaction goes to the head teller, who writes it in the day book in order; the assistants copy the day book line by line. Telling a customer "done" as soon as the head teller has written the line is w: 1. Waiting until at least one assistant has copied it too is w: "majority". If the head teller is locked in the back office, the two assistants agree that one of them takes over, because two of three is a majority. When the head teller comes out, any lines only they wrote get torn out and filed in an envelope, since the branch now follows the new day book. The analogy breaks on the envelope: in MongoDB nobody reads it unless an operator goes looking, and the customer who was told "done" is never called back.
world: Before you add MongoDB, ask whether a JSON column in the database you already run would do: Oracle has had JSON columns and JSON_TABLE for years, and the PostgreSQL side of this lesson carries over. Your Oracle primary with a Data Guard standby in maximum availability mode is the same idea as w: "majority": commit waits for the standby, so a failover loses nothing. A Quarkus service using the MongoDB Java driver gets w: "majority" by default; the danger is someone setting w: 1 "for speed" on the payments collection. Embed refunds and the status history in the payment document and use guarded single-document updates, and you need no transaction for the refund rule. When a write fails with a write concern timeout, treat it like a timeout from the card issuer: the write may have happened. A Temporal activity that retries it should use the payment id as _id or check an idempotency key with a partial unique index, so the retry can't create a second payment.
mistake: The most common mistake is treating acknowledged: true as "durable", and lowering the write concern to w: 1 for throughput. In a healthy set nothing looks wrong, and the latency gain is real but small, a few milliseconds. Then a primary is cut off for a few seconds, takes writes no one else sees, and rolls them back when it rejoins. Payments the service confirmed vanish, with no error anywhere, and the only trace is a BSON file in a rollback directory. The fix: keep w: "majority" (the default since 5.0) for anything that matters, treat a write concern timeout as unknown rather than failed, and read with majority where acting on a rolled-back write would hurt.

compare.title: A merchant's daily totals: SQL and the aggregation pipeline

a.label: SQL (PostgreSQL or Oracle)
a.title: SQL (PostgreSQL or Oracle)
a.html: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS payments, SUM(amount_minor) AS amount_minor, MAX(amount_minor) AS largest FROM payment WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042' AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2026-11-07 00:00:00' AND created_at < TIMESTAMP '2026-11-08 00:00:00' GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

b.label: MongoDB aggregation
b.title: MongoDB aggregation
b.html: db.payments.aggregate([ { $match: { merchantId: "M-0042", // WHERE createdAt: { $gte: ISODate("2026-11-07T00:00:00Z"), $lt: ISODate("2026-11-08T00:00:00Z") } } }, { $group: { _id: "$status", // GROUP BY payments: { $sum: 1 }, // COUNT(*) amountMinor: { $sum: "$amountMinor" }, // SUM largest: { $max: "$amountMinor" } } }, // MAX { $sort: { _id: 1 } } // ORDER BY ])

compare.note: The two say the same thing, and both planners use an index for the WHERE part. The difference is the order. SQL is declarative: the optimizer decides when to filter, group and sort. A pipeline runs its stages in the order you write them, with a few rewrites by the server, so $match belongs first or the index can't help. And a pipeline passes documents, not rows: $group can build arrays ($push) and nested results that SQL would need a second query or JSON functions for.

worked.title: Shape the payment document and its indexes from the access patterns

steps.say: Start from lesson 2's access patterns and mark which document answers each one. AP1 stays on the account document, with its capped summary of recent payments.
steps.code:
AP1  account's recent payments    accounts doc, recentPayments ($push + $slice)
AP2  payment by id                payments._id
AP3  merchant + status, newest     index { merchantId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 }
AP4  idempotency key used once     unique partial index on idempotencyKey
AP6  refunds of a payment          embedded in the payment (bounded)

steps.say: Write one payment the way it will be stored. Amounts are 64-bit integers in minor units, times are dates, refunds are inside, with the running total next to them.
steps.code: { _id: "pay-81723", accountId: "A-1001", merchantId: "M-0042", status: "SETTLED", amountMinor: NumberLong(4250), currency: "EUR", createdAt: ISODate("2026-11-07T09:00:00Z"), idempotencyKey: "idem-7f3a", refundedMinor: NumberLong(1250), refunds: [ { refundId: "ref-1", amountMinor: NumberLong(1250), at: ISODate("2026-11-07T10:02:00Z") } ] }

steps.say: Make the shape a rule. The validator fixes the types and bounds the array, which is what made embedding safe. On 9.0, upgrade an existing collection to constraint once it's clean.
steps.code: db.createCollection("payments", { validator: { $jsonSchema: { bsonType: "object", required: ["accountId", "merchantId", "status", "amountMinor", "createdAt", "refundedMinor", "refunds"], properties: { status: { enum: ["AUTHORIZED", "SETTLED", "FAILED"] }, amountMinor: { bsonType: "long", minimum: 1 }, refundedMinor: { bsonType: "long", minimum: 0 }, refunds: { bsonType: "array", maxItems: 20 } } } } })

steps.say: Create one index per pattern that isn't _id, and nothing else. Each one is a sorted list every write has to maintain.
steps.code: db.payments.createIndex({ merchantId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 }) // AP3 db.payments.createIndex({ idempotencyKey: 1 }, // AP4 { unique: true, partialFilterExpression: { idempotencyKey: { $type: "string" } } }) db.payments.createIndex({ "refunds.refundId": 1 }) // support: refund -> payment

steps.say: Check each pattern with explain() before you ship. You want an IXSCAN, no SORT, and keys examined close to documents returned.
steps.code: cost(db.payments.find({ merchantId: "M-0042", status: "FAILED" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(5)) // { plan: 'LIMIT > FETCH > IXSCAN', returned: 5, keysExamined: 5, docsExamined: 5 }

lab.title: Store payments as documents: embed, guard, index, aggregate
steps: Make sure Docker is running, then run the tests from the labs folder. The first run starts one mongo:9.0 container through Testcontainers (a few seconds, plus the pull if you've never run env/mongo.yml). All nine tests fail.
Read PaymentDocs.kt. The schema and createCollection are given; every test writes into a collection with that validator, in a database of its own.
Write toDocument first: every other test seeds its data with it. The first two tests check the stored BSON types and that the validator accepts your documents and rejects bad ones.
Write addRefund as one updateOne with a guarded filter. The race test fires twenty refunds at once at a 10,000 payment and expects exactly ten to win.

Write createIndexes, recentByMerchantStatus and dailyTotalsPipeline. The tests run explain() on your query and your pipeline and check for an IXSCAN, no SORT, and 5 keys and 5 documents for 5 results. Swap status and createdAt in your index and watch the AP3 test fail.
hints: Document("_id", p.paymentId).append(...). A Kotlin Long becomes BSON long; Date.from(instant) becomes a BSON date. The refunds are p.refunds.map(::refundDocument).

The guard compares two fields of the same document, so it needs Filters.expr: Document("\$lte", listOf(Document("\$add", listOf("\$refundedMinor", refund.amountMinor)), "\$amountMinor")). Return modifiedCount == 1L.

The pipeline is listOf(Aggregates.match(...), Aggregates.group("\$status", Accumulators.sum("count", 1), ...), Aggregates.sort(Sorts.ascending("_id"))). The day runs from day.atStartOfDay(ZoneOffset.UTC) to the next day's start, end excluded.

drill.title: The guarded refund and the write concerns, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the mongosh updateOne that adds a 1,250 refund ref-2 to payment pay-81723 only if the payment is SETTLED and the refunds stay within the amount. Then write one line each: what w: 1 and w: "majority" promise when the client hears OK, and what happens to each if the primary is cut off right after.

answer.html: db.payments.updateOne( { _id: "pay-81723", status: "SETTLED", $expr: { $lte: [{ $add: ["$refundedMinor", 1250] }, "$amountMinor"] } }, // the guard { $push: { refunds: { refundId: "ref-2", amountMinor: NumberLong(1250), at: new Date() } }, $inc: { refundedMinor: NumberLong(1250) } }) // one document: atomic // modifiedCount 1: applied. 0: not settled, or it would refund too much. // w: 1 the primary has it. Cut off now: rolled back when it rejoins, client never told. // w: "majority" 2 of 3 members have it. Cut off now: any new primary has it too. It survives. // wtimeout hit error to the client, but the write isn't undone: treat it as unknown.

recap: A MongoDB document is a BSON tree with typed fields, an _id and a 16 MB limit. A write to one document is atomic, so embed what's read and changed together and bounded, like a payment's refunds, and guard the change in the update's filter.
Validators give collections a schema: strict checks every write, and 9.0's constraint level also checks every existing document before it switches on. Failed writes get error 121.

A PostgreSQL jsonb column is the same model inside a table: one guarded UPDATE is atomic, a CHECK constraint plays the validator (NOT VALID for new rows only), and joins and multi-row transactions come for free. MongoDB adds path indexes in sorted order and sharding.

explain() tells you what a query read: IXSCAN keys, FETCHed documents, COLLSCAN, in-memory SORT. Covered queries read no documents, array fields make multikey indexes, and a unique index on an optional field must be partial.
An aggregation pipeline passes documents through stages: $match, $group, $sort, $project, $unwind, $lookup. Put $match first so an index can serve it.
A replica set has one primary that orders writes in its oplog. w: "majority" (the default since 5.0) survives failover; a w: 1 write can be rolled back into a file, with no error to the client.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to set w: 1 on the payments collection because "we measured 3 ms faster writes, and acknowledged is acknowledged". Explain what w: 1 and w: "majority" each promise, and what happens to a w: 1 payment in a failover.
explain.answer: With w: 1 the client hears OK as soon as the primary has the write in its oplog. With w: "majority" it waits until two of our three members have it, which in a healthy set costs a few milliseconds. The difference only shows in a failover. If the primary is cut off, the other two elect a new primary after about 10 seconds, and a member only votes for a candidate whose oplog is at least as recent as its own, so every majority-acknowledged write is on the new primary. A w: 1 write that hadn't reached a secondary isn't. When the old primary rejoins, it finds the last oplog entry it shares with the new primary and rolls back everything after it into a BSON file in its rollback directory. The payment we confirmed is simply gone from the collection, and no client gets an error. Three milliseconds isn't worth that for payments. Keep the default w: "majority", and treat a write concern timeout as unknown, because the write isn't undone either.

deeper.html:
Read concern and write concern combine. MongoDB's causally consistent sessions promise read-your-writes and monotonic reads across members, but the defaults page is precise about when: only if the session's reads use majority read concern and its writes use majority write concern. With the defaults, reads use local, which "can return data that may be rolled back". The Replication track's lesson on follower lag names these guarantees and shows where each one breaks.

Jepsen's 2020 analysis of MongoDB 4.2.6 is the cautionary tale. Transactions ignored the database and collection defaults and fell back to local reads and w: 1 writes unless the transaction set its own concerns, and Jepsen lost acknowledged writes under network partitions. Read skew and other anomalies showed up even at the strongest settings, which MongoDB traced to a retry bug with a fix scheduled for 4.2.8. The recommendation still stands for every version: set read and write concern explicitly on each transaction, snapshot and majority.

In 2012 Abadi's PACELC paper classed MongoDB as PA/EC, partly because of its asynchronous replication and its "rollback directory". The default became w: "majority" in 5.0, so the class describes a configuration of its time, not the product. The Consistency and consensus track's first lesson uses PACELC properly.

The oplog is a capped collection: when it's full, the oldest entries go. A secondary that falls further behind than the oldest entry can't catch up by replaying and needs a full initial sync. Size the oplog for your longest expected outage, maintenance window included.

Arbiters are members that vote but hold no data. With two data members and one arbiter, a majority of data-bearing members is impossible during a failure, so MongoDB's implicit default write concern drops to w: 1 for such sets. That's one more reason to run three data-bearing members.

Elections in more detail: the MongoDB docs say an election should typically finish within 12 seconds, a primary that can see only a minority of members steps down by itself, and reads have their own dial, the read concern. local, the default, can return writes that are later rolled back; majority returns only what a majority holds; linearizable reads from the primary and sees every majority write that finished before the read began.
